So, after plowing through today's (Sunday)'s puzzle with brute force and second-hand knowledge of video-gaming; and wanting to save Monday's for tomorrow's lunch-break, I decided, while eating dinner tonight, to do a puzzle from the archives--in particular, Saturday, Dec. 29, 2018 B.E. I completed it in about 2/3 of yesterday's time, just over last Saturday's, and less than half of my average*. And all of this while eating forkfuls of mushroom fettuccine. But here's the thing--it was by Robyn Weintraub, and full of punchy entries which brought a smile to my pasta-filled face! I also read Wordplay, and the comments--Caitlyn was already dropping visual spoilers in her lead photo (or is it lede photo, Barry?); among the commenters were @BA, @MOL (not so O, but just as M), @RiA, @Lewis; and others whom we seldom if ever see anymore--@Andrew in Ottawa, @DC. (I was so tempted to write a snarky reply to @DC, but then thought, What's the point?) And guess what? People were complaining that it was too easy! La plus ça change. https://www.nytimes.com/crosswords/game/daily/2018/12/29 *I don't really trust "averages"--after all, one's skill is always improving, and one is always leaving one's laptop open.

@J-J Cote you decimate by taking every tenth. Whether you keep or discard your selection, either way the operation is the same. In data streams you decimate by throwing away 9 out of 10 samples.

"The Origin of "Ti" and "So"English Innovation: John Curwen introduced "ti" in 19th-century England for his Tonic Sol-fa system so that every solfège syllable would start with a unique consonant letter (D, R, M, F, S, L, T)."So" vs "Sol": Dropping the final "-l" in "sol" is an English phonetic shortening; the original 11th-century Latin syllable established by Guido d'Arezzo ends with an 'l'.
